summary: Describes Path MTU Discovery for IPv6, derived largely from the IPv4 version in RFC 1191. It lets a sender learn the largest packet that can cross a path without being broken up. It was replaced by RFC 8201.

eli5.summary: Before mailing a big box, you want to know the narrowest door along the way. This is how computers find out the largest package that fits.

questions: what is ipv6 path mtu discovery
how does pmtud work in ipv6
what is an icmpv6 packet too big message
what is the minimum mtu in ipv6
subtitle: How an IPv6 sender finds the largest packet that fits along a whole path, using Packet Too Big messages.

tldr.problem: Sending the biggest packets that a path can carry gives the best use of the network, but a sender does not know the smallest link size along the way.
tldr.mechanism: The sender starts with the MTU of its first hop. A node that cannot forward a packet discards it and returns an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message carrying the next-hop MTU, and the sender lowers its estimate.
tldr.outcome: Path MTU Discovery is optional for IPv6 nodes (SHOULD, not MUST), and nodes that skip it use the IPv6 minimum link MTU. This RFC was replaced by RFC 8201.

today: RFC 1981 is a Draft Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8201, which is the document to consult for current IPv6 Path MTU Discovery.

sections.title: The Path MTU Problem
sections.content:
When one IPv6 node has a lot of data for another, it sends a series of packets. Those packets are best made as large as the path can carry. That size is the Path MTU (PMTU), which equals the minimum link MTU of all the links on the path.

IPv6 nodes SHOULD implement Path MTU Discovery to take advantage of paths larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU, though a minimal implementation (for example in a boot ROM) may omit it. Nodes that skip it use the IPv6 minimum link MTU as the maximum packet size. That is safe but usually wasteful, because most paths allow bigger packets.

The RFC is largely derived from RFC 1191, which describes the same idea for IPv4.
sections.eli5: A truck should carry as much as the narrowest bridge on its route allows. If it always assumes the tiniest bridge, it makes far too many trips.

sections.title: How Discovery Works
sections.content:
The source node begins by assuming the PMTU equals the known MTU of the first hop. If a packet is too large for some node on the path, that node discards it and returns an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message. The source then lowers its assumed PMTU to the MTU reported in the message. Several rounds can occur, because a smaller link may lie further along.

Discovery ends when the estimate is less than or equal to the actual PMTU. A node can also end it by sending nothing larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU.

Paths change, so the PMTU can change. Decreases show up through Packet Too Big messages. To notice increases, a node periodically tries a larger size, which usually fails, so it should be done infrequently. For multicast, one packet can draw several Packet Too Big messages, and the smallest PMTU across the paths in use sets the size of later packets. Discovery must also be done when a destination seems to be on the same link, since a neighboring router acting as proxy can hide a destination that is really more than one hop away.
sections.eli5: You send a package. If it is too wide for a door, the door-keeper sends it back with a note giving the door's width. You repack to that size and try again.

sections.title: Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
These rules apply only to implementations that include Path MTU Discovery.

  • On receiving a Packet Too Big message, a node MUST reduce its PMTU estimate to the value of the MTU field, and MUST reduce the packets it sends on that path to avoid more such messages.
  • Nodes MUST detect decreases as fast as possible. They MAY probe for increases, but MUST NOT do so less than 5 minutes after a Packet Too Big message for that path; the recommended timer is twice the minimum, 10 minutes.
  • A node MUST NOT reduce its estimate below the IPv6 minimum link MTU. If a message reports a smaller next-hop MTU, the node includes a Fragment header in packets instead.
  • A node MUST NOT increase its estimate because of a Packet Too Big message, since such a message might be stale, forged in a denial-of-service attack, or caused by multiple paths with different PMTUs.
sections.eli5: Always listen when told your package is too big, never shrink below the smallest allowed size, and only rarely test whether a bigger size would now work.

sections.title: Implementation Notes: Layers, Caching and Aging
sections.content:
Section 5 is advice for implementors, not a specification. It suggests that the IP layer store PMTU information and the ICMP layer process Packet Too Big messages, while the upper layers (called packetization layers) adapt the size of what they send. Layers learn a derived value, MMS_S, the maximum send transport-message size, which is the PMTU minus the IPv6 header and any space the IP layer reserves for additional headers. Applications that cannot change their message size can rely on IPv6 fragmentation, but they are encouraged to avoid it.

Since a node rarely knows the exact path, it keeps a PMTU against a local representation of a path. The choices range from one value for the whole node, to one per destination address, to one per flow id, optionally refined by a source route. Initially the value is the first-hop MTU.

Cached values go stale. A too-large value is found quickly, but a too-small one is not, so an implementation should age entries: when a value has not been decreased for around 10 minutes, it is reset to the first-hop MTU. One suggested design records a timestamp and runs a timer-driven procedure once a minute over the cache. There should be a way to change the timeout, including to infinity, and for an administrator to disable discovery on a path or set its PMTU.
sections.eli5: The computer keeps a notebook of the biggest package that worked for each destination, and every so often it crosses an entry out and tries again in case the road got wider.

sections.title: TCP and Other Transports
sections.content:
TCP must track the PMTU of the path in use and should not send segments that would produce larger packets. It must also respect the MSS value received from its peer. The MSS option TCP sends is independent of the PMTU, because the other end may be using an unrelated PMTU.

A Packet Too Big message means a packet was dropped, so TCP can treat it like any dropped segment and wait for the retransmission timer. Alternatively it can retransmit immediately, only for the affected connection and no larger than the new PMTU. It must not retransmit for every message in a burst, or the number of extra segments would grow exponentially. Such a retransmission should not change the congestion window but should trigger slow start.

Some transports, such as ISO TP4, cannot repacketize on retransmission, so IP may fragment the original segment. Sun NFS over UDP often generates payloads that need fragmentation even for the first-hop link, which is known to cause reliability and performance problems, so NFS implementations are recommended to use Path MTU Discovery whenever routers are involved.
sections.eli5: If a package comes back as too big, repack it once at the new size. Do not keep re-sending the same big one over and over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism allows two denial-of-service attacks, both using forged Packet Too Big messages.

In the first, the message claims a PMTU much smaller than reality. This cannot stop data flow completely, because the victim never goes below the IPv6 minimum link MTU, but it hurts performance. In the second, the message claims a PMTU larger than reality, which could cause temporary blockage until the victim learns better within about one round-trip time. A node that never raises its estimate based on a Packet Too Big message is not vulnerable to this second attack.

An attacker who could stop legitimate Packet Too Big messages from arriving could cause problems too, but simpler denial-of-service attacks exist in that case.
sections.eli5: A prankster could send fake notes saying doors are tiny. That makes you slow, but you never go below the smallest allowed size, and you ignore notes claiming doors got bigger.
